why: Telemetry for the partition case, and the corpus's first whose readings describe **two authorities at once**. Every earlier case measures one component getting worse; here the member count is three because a member can only see its own side of a fork, and the election counter moved twice because each half held its own vote. `stale_read_ratio` is the number that makes the difference operational: an unavailable cluster returns nothing and pages, a forked cluster returns yesterday's answer and is believed. The two configuration facts carry the parts of the ticket that are not measurements -- one firmware roll, seventeen minutes -- and they are declared rather than modelled as series because a roll is an event and a duration is an interval between two events, neither of which has samples. Everything is recorded against the cluster rather than against a node, and that is a limit rather than a choice: `signalRef` is one name resolved across the case, so 'the members each side sees' cannot be two series with one name, and a partition's two viewpoints are therefore one series and one prose sentence. The guard refuses two series with one name outright (finding 299 records why that refusal is the honest one, and what it costs).

series.quote: The search cluster split into two sides at 03:02 and each side elected its own leader
series.why: the checkpoint `cp-members-halved` holds the value: three is one side's view of a six-node cluster that became two three-node clusters

series.quote: each side elected its own leader
series.why: the checkpoint `cp-two-elections` holds the difference: two elections in seventeen minutes, one per side, which is the count that separates a split from a failover

series.quote: Queries on one side returned documents that the other side had already deleted
series.why: the checkpoint `cp-stale-reads` holds the value: the half that never saw a delete answers confidently, which is why a partition reads as a data-quality problem before it reads as an outage
